sections.h2: Who handles what in a Daytona Beach sale
sections.html:
County government covers Daytona Beach for property values, tax bills and deed recording. The city itself issues permits, runs rental registration and enforces codes. Sorting out which desk keeps which record will save you many calls.

The house itself points to a route. A well-kept home near the water may do well listed, but a rental, an estate property or a place with heavy repairs is more likely to suit a direct purchase as-is.

  • An agent fits a house that shows well when waiting on a financed buyer is acceptable.
  • A for-sale-by-owner sale works for people who handle contracts and disclosure forms without stress.
  • Cash makes sense when time, condition or tenants stand in the way.

Daytona Beach landlords do have to register. The City Commission dropped the old Residential License Program in 2024 and put in a rental registration rule for owners holding fewer than five units. It renews every year and covers long-term rentals, meaning leases of six months plus one day or more.

Rental registration charges, City of Daytona Beach Rental Property Program
Registration chargeAmount
First-time application$40
First registration, each unit$50
Yearly registration, each unit$75

A voluntary inspection is available, and passing it waives the following year's fee. If you want stays shorter than six months plus one day, phone the Business Tax Office at (386) 671-8140 to learn whether your zoning allows it. The Rental Property Program office is at 125 S. Palmetto Ave.

Selling a rental? Renew the registration first, since a buyer or title agent may want to see it. Note that the program covers long-term leases only, so short stays need zoning confirmation of their own.

Around November 1 the Volusia tax collector mails bills. You can pay without penalty until March 31.

  • The discount is 4 percent in November, 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February, and nothing in March.
  • March 31 is also the deferral application deadline.
  • Accounts turn delinquent April 1, when a minimum 3 percent charge is added.
  • A new installment plan has to be requested by April 30.

After April 30, unpaid accounts are advertised and head toward the yearly certificate sale. The certificate becomes a first lien and, two years on, supports a tax deed application, so pay off any balance by closing day.

The appraiser's exemption deadline is March 1, as elsewhere in the state. Homestead can lower assessed value by up to $50,000.

A permit left open, or a pending code case, will probably appear when a buyer does due diligence. City Code Compliance staff look for blighted or substandard housing and push for its repair or removal.

Pull the permit history for your address before you list. Anything done without a final sign-off, whether a new roof, a new room or electrical or plumbing changes, should be cleaned up first. Cash buyers accept the house's flaws, yet the title company still wants liens and open cases paid or accounted for.

Ask the city for any unpaid code charges when you collect payoff figures. They can stay with the parcel and appear in a title search.

Volusia County runs notices on delinquent accounts three times, in the newspaper and online, after April 30. The advertising and auction listing fees are tacked onto the tax notice, and they cannot be removed after it runs, which is a reason to pay before the deadline.

A bill still open at the annual certificate sale leads the county to sell a certificate against the parcel, and further charges pile up. Redeeming takes guaranteed funds, though the collector also accepts credit or debit cards.

Under state law, the certificate holder can pursue a tax deed once two years have run from April 1 of the issue year. On a homestead, the opening bid counts half the latest assessed value. With a certificate outstanding, ask the tax collector for the redemption total and plan to pay it out of your proceeds.

Deferral works differently. By March 31, homestead owners may submit Form DR-570 to the collector, postponing the tax that exceeds a set share of household income.

When the deed is recorded, the clerk's office takes the tax. It is priced per $100 of consideration under section 201.02, and the state revenue page lists county rates, with Miami-Dade the odd one out.

State rules make everyone on the deed liable, which leaves the contract to decide who actually pays. Section 28.24 recording charges are billed page by page.

Whether it is a warranty, special warranty, quitclaim or trustee's deed, the tax applies. Any such transfer also resets assessed value to just value on the next New Year's Day.

Three deadlines come up most often: foreclosure sales, probate and tenant notices.

After a foreclosure judgment, the clerk's sale is set about three to five weeks away, and the high bidder puts down 5 percent. Objections to the bid must come within 10 days.

Probate is the first step for an inherited house. A summary administration is possible if non-exempt assets are $150,000 or under, or the owner died over two years earlier. Creditors who miss the claim deadline lose their claims.

A tenant behind on rent receives a written notice allowing three days. Once the court orders removal, the sheriff posts a 24-hour notice. When the house is under lease at sale, record in writing whether the buyer will keep the lease.

After you accept an offer, a title company examines the record, clears liens and drafts the deed. On your side, collect the lender's payoff letter, your most recent tax bill and any association paperwork. Put in writing who covers the title policy and recording. Weigh each offer against the net an agent listing would leave once repairs, fees and holding costs come out.

Before the signing appointment, read the settlement statement closely, confirm where your proceeds will be sent, and bring photo ID. Hand over keys, garage openers and any gate codes at closing, and keep copies of everything you sign. Do not cancel your homeowner's insurance until the deed is recorded.

If anything in the file is unclear, such as a name that differs between the deed and your tax bill, ask the title agent about it early. Fixing a mismatch before contract is far easier than during a title review, and it keeps a short timeline from slipping. Ask for your closing figures a day ahead so you are not reading them for the first time at the table.

faqs.q: Is rental registration required in Daytona Beach?
faqs.a: Yes, for owners of fewer than five residential units under the 2024 ordinance. The yearly fee is $75 per unit after the first year, and passing a voluntary inspection waives the following year's fee.

faqs.q: When do Volusia County taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: April 1. A 3 percent minimum charge is added then, and accounts unpaid after April 30 are advertised and can go to the certificate sale.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Daytona Beach house with an unregistered rental?
faqs.a: You can, though registering first is wise. Buyers and title agents may want proof the rental complies.

faqs.q: Who collects the deed tax on a Daytona Beach sale?
faqs.a: The county clerk collects it at recording. Section 201.02 sets it per $100 of consideration, and your sale contract says which side pays.

faqs.q: Does selling end my homestead protection?
faqs.a: Yes. The Save Our Homes cap ends at a change of ownership, and the buyer starts at just value the next January 1. If you are buying another Florida home, the Volusia County Property Appraiser can explain portability.
